summary: This document defines requirements for Distributed Mobility Management at the network layer. Traditional wireless networks rely on centrally placed mobility anchors, but as networks flatten, it can help to spread mobility functions so traffic need not pass through a central point.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move around with your phone, someone keeps track of where to send your data. Instead of one big office doing it for everyone, this RFC asks what is needed to share the job across many places.

subtitle: Why mobility anchors should move closer to users, and the eight requirements any distributed mobility solution must meet.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks rely on a few centrally placed mobility anchors that carry the traffic of millions of mobile nodes, which causes non-optimal routes, scaling limits and a single point of failure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares centralized and distributed mobility management, lists eight problems (PS1 to PS8) and sets out eight requirements (REQ1 to REQ8) that network-layer distributed mobility management (DMM) solutions must follow.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements only and specifies no protocol. It is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 7333 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for DMM and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why Distribute Mobility Management
sections.content:
Network-layer mobility protocols such as Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6 all use a mobility anchor that keeps a mobile node reachable after it moves to a different network, and forwards packets to or from it. In today's deployments there are only a few anchors, and one anchor typically manages the traffic of millions of mobile nodes. When a subscriber roams, the anchor may still sit in the home provider's network so that charging and billing are easier.

The RFC gives two reasons to look at an alternative. Mobile users consume more Internet content, including from local Content Delivery Networks, and mobile networks are being flattened, so anchoring traffic nearer to the user makes sense. Also, mobile nodes often stay at the same point of attachment for long periods, yet mobility support is built for always-on operation and keeps context for every subscriber. That can waste resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now a few giant post offices handle everyone's forwarded mail. This RFC asks what we need so that many small local post offices could do it instead.

sections.title: Centralized versus Distributed
sections.content:
IP-layer mobility works by separating a session identifier (the node's original address) from a forwarding address (its new address after moving) and keeping a mapping between the two. Packets sent to the session identifier go first to the original network, which redirects them, and that can make routes long.

In centralized mobility management, the mapping lives at a single anchor and packets go through it, so both control plane and data plane are centralized. Examples are the home agent and local mobility anchor, and the 3GPP GPRS and EPS gateway hierarchies. In distributed mobility management, the functions are spread through the data plane so a node is served by a nearby forwarding-management function. The control plane may be either centralized or distributed. Other functions, such as subscription databases and network access authentication, need not be distributed.

The RFC recommends first considering whether existing mobility protocols can be extended before designing new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Centralized means all forwarded mail goes through one far-away office. Distributed means a nearby office can handle it.

sections.title: The Eight Problems
sections.content:
Section 4 lists problems that DMM could address:

  • PS1: non-optimal routes, which increase end-to-end delay.
  • PS2: divergence from the trend toward flatter networks and distributed content delivery.
  • PS3: poor scalability of centralized tunnel management and mobility context maintenance.
  • PS4: a single point of failure and attack.
  • PS5: mobility support given to nodes and sessions that do not need it.
  • PS6: mobility signaling overhead for peer-to-peer communication.
  • PS7: hard deployment alongside multiple existing mobility solutions.
  • PS8: duplicate multicast traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight things go wrong with one giant office: long detours, no room to grow, one thing that can break everything, and doing extra work for people who did not need it.

sections.title: The Eight Requirements
sections.content:
Each requirement comes with a motivation and the problems it addresses.

  • REQ1, distributed mobility management. Solutions MUST let traffic avoid traversing a single mobility anchor far from the optimal route. This applies to the data plane only. It addresses PS1 to PS4.
  • REQ2, bypassable mobility support. Network-layer mobility MUST be enabled, but any individual active session MUST be able to not use it. Addresses PS5 and PS6.
  • REQ3, IPv6 deployment. Solutions SHOULD target IPv6 as the primary environment and SHOULD NOT be tailored specifically for IPv4.
  • REQ4, existing protocols. A solution MUST first consider reusing and extending IETF standard protocols.
  • REQ5, coexistence. Solutions MUST coexist with existing deployments, hosts and routers, and SHOULD work across administrative domains where trust allows. Addresses PS7.
  • REQ6, operation and management. Solutions need to consider configuration, monitoring and fault handling, for example with SNMP, NETCONF with YANG, syslog or IPFIX. They MUST describe how they scale and MUST support ways to test that they work.
  • REQ7, security. Solutions MUST support the needed security mechanisms and MUST NOT introduce new risks, or amplify existing ones, that existing mechanisms cannot mitigate.
  • REQ8, multicast. DMM SHOULD enable multicast solutions that avoid network inefficiency. Addresses PS1 and PS8.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: do not force every message through a far-away office, let people skip the service when they do not need it, build on what already works, play nicely with old equipment, make it easy to check, keep it safe, and handle group messages well.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The security section only points to REQ7. REQ7's motivation lists attacks such as impersonation, denial of service and man-in-the-middle, including a malicious node forging signaling messages to redirect traffic away from its legitimate path. The RFC expects existing protections for access control, integrity, authentication, authorization and confidentiality to be used. If a candidate DMM solution cannot be secured even with those mechanisms used properly, it is said to cause uncontrollable security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor could trick the mail system into sending your mail to the wrong place, so any new design must be safe from that.
